intro: At C1 you explained Indonesian ideas like sungkan and musyawarah, and you helped two colleagues who disagreed. Now you become the bridge between whole cultures: you explain how people tend to behave and why, choose between direct and indirect politeness for each listener, and make sure that a polite 'iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' isn't heard as a firm yes.
teachingNotes: Recap in a line, don't re-teach: from c1-mediation-synthesis the learner explains a cultural concept in four parts (approximate translation, real example, what it isn't, why it matters) and already knows sungkan, gotong royong, musyawarah, jam karet, mudik and basa-basi, plus the five mediator moves (restate neutrally, common ground, separate people from the problem, a way forward, check both accept); from c2-implied-meaning they decode the polite code (I'm not sure that's the best idea = I disagree), know when to be indirect and when to be direct (safety, money, deadlines), the Indonesian code (iya = I hear you, nanti dulu = a soft no, boleh juga = a careful yes) and silence/subtext; from b2-small-talk-networking safe vs sensitive topics; from c1-register Mr / Ms + surname. New here: explaining NORMS (unwritten rules of behaviour) in both directions, comparing politeness strategies, and bridging meaning between two sides of a conversation.

Explaining a norm (objective explain-norms): tendency + reason + what it doesn't mean + what to do. Tendency words: many, often, tend to, in some workplaces, it's common to; never always / never / all Indonesians / the Dutch are…, and never better / worse / more advanced. Facts to get right: Pak/Bu + FIRST name (Pak Budi) because many Indonesians have no family name (so Mr Budi is fine in English for an Indonesian colleague; for Westerners Mr / Ms + surname, never Mr John); first names even with the CEO are common in Australia and the Netherlands; many traditional German companies still use Herr / Frau + surname (direct is not the same as informal). Age is asked partly to know how to address someone (Mbak, Kak, Dik, Bu, Pak); salary, marriage and weight questions are friendly attention in Indonesia but sensitive in many Western workplaces. Friday prayers around midday (many workplaces take a longer break, roughly 11.30 to 1); daily prayers take about 10-15 minutes, often in the musholla; Ramadan fasting from dawn to sunset, shorter office hours in many places, buka puasa bersama; halal food when hosting. Gifts: oleh-oleh (Japanese omiyage is similar); gifts are often opened later, not in front of the giver, in Indonesia and Japan, while many Australians open them straight away. Give and receive with the right hand (or both hands for extra respect); Japanese business cards with both hands. Criticism tends to be private in Indonesian, Japanese and Thai settings; open disagreement with a manager is often normal in Dutch workplaces.

Politeness strategies (objective politeness-strategies), plainly, no heavy theory: low-context (Edward T. Hall) = the message is mostly in the words; high-context = much of it is in the relationship, the situation and what isn't said. Positive politeness (Brown and Levinson) = showing closeness (first names, compliments, we, personal interest); negative politeness = not imposing (options, apologies, could you possibly…); negative does NOT mean bad. Broad tendencies only: Dutch, German and Australian speakers more direct; Japanese, Thai and Indonesian speakers more indirect; Americans are explicit but often wrap criticism in praise. Directness and formality are two different scales. Choosing: the listener, the relationship and hierarchy, public or private, and the stakes (costly misunderstandings need clear content). Rule of thumb: adapt the form, keep the content clear.

Bridging meaning (objective bridge-meaning). The node's common error: translating a polite 'iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' (or kami usahakan, agak sulit, Pak) as a firm yes. The fix is NOT to turn every iya into a no: interpret with a hedge (So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean he has some concerns), then check with the speaker, often privately (Could I check what you meant by …? / What would make this work for your team?), then confirm in writing. Insyaallah is a sincere expression of faith; its meaning ranges from yes to a polite maybe, so check, never mock it, and don't test it. Reframing: keep the content, change the packaging (It's about the report, not about you. Her main point is …), and the other way make an indirect message explicit for a direct listener (What Mr Sato is telling us, politely, is that the price is too high). Silence may mean thinking, respect for a senior person or quiet disagreement, not agreement: ask by name, give time, follow up privately. A mediator never takes sides and never says one culture is better.

Limits and grading: all grammar is available, but this is a mediation lesson, not grammar; don't teach negotiation tactics (c1-negotiation), Hofstede's dimensions, honorific systems (keigo) or religious rules beyond the workplace facts above. Contexts: a Dutch manager (Anna) and an Indonesian team in Jakarta, a Japanese client (Mr Sato) visiting a factory in Cikarang, an Australian NGO (Kate) in Lombok. When the learner practises, play the foreign colleague or the Indonesian colleague, react to the content, then correct ONE thing (usually a stereotype word like always, a word-for-word translation of a soft no, taking sides, or changing the content while reframing). Accept any natural wording with the right move or meaning; many choices are style: only mark clear errors.

keyPoints.title: Explain a norm: tendency, reason, what it isn't, what to do
keyPoints.explanation: A norm is an unwritten rule about how people behave. Explain it as a tendency (In many Indonesian offices…, People often…, In some workplaces…), give the value behind it (respect, harmony, closeness, efficiency), say what it doesn't mean (It isn't rudeness / It doesn't mean they're not interested) and what to do (So it's a good idea to…). Work in both directions: Indonesian norms for foreign colleagues and foreign norms for Indonesian colleagues. Never always / never / all, and never say one culture is better.

examples.en: In many Indonesian offices, people keep using Pak or Bu with your first name, even after you say 'Call me Kate'. It feels polite to them, not cold.
examples.id: Di banyak kantor di Indonesia, orang tetap memakai Pak atau Bu dengan nama depanmu, meskipun kamu sudah bilang 'Call me Kate'. Bagi mereka itu sopan, bukan dingin.

examples.en: In many Dutch workplaces, disagreeing openly with your manager is normal. It isn't a personal attack.
examples.id: Di banyak tempat kerja di Belanda, membantah manajer secara terbuka itu biasa. Itu bukan serangan pribadi.

examples.en: Lombok is mostly Muslim, so on Fridays it's a good idea to finish the morning session by 11.30.
examples.id: Mayoritas penduduk Lombok Muslim, jadi pada hari Jumat sebaiknya sesi pagi selesai paling lambat pukul 11.30.

id.title: Jelaskan norma: kecenderungan, alasan, apa yang bukan, apa yang perlu dilakukan
id.explanation: Norma adalah aturan tak tertulis tentang cara orang bersikap. Jelaskan sebagai kecenderungan (In many Indonesian offices…, People often…, In some workplaces…), sebutkan nilai di baliknya (hormat, kerukunan, keakraban, efisiensi), katakan apa yang bukan maksudnya (It isn't rudeness / It doesn't mean they're not interested) dan apa yang sebaiknya dilakukan (So it's a good idea to…). Lakukan ke dua arah: norma Indonesia untuk rekan asing, dan norma asing untuk rekan Indonesia. Jangan pakai always / never / all, dan jangan pernah bilang satu budaya lebih baik.

keyPoints.title: Direct or indirect: choose the strategy for the listener
keyPoints.explanation: In low-context communication the message is mostly in the words; in high-context communication much of it is in the relationship, the situation and what isn't said. Positive politeness shows closeness (first names, compliments, we); negative politeness avoids imposing (options, apologies, Could you possibly…?). As broad tendencies, Dutch, German and Australian speakers are more direct, Japanese, Thai and Indonesian speakers more indirect. Choose for the listener, the relationship, public or private, and the stakes: adapt the form, keep the content clear.

examples.en: The shipment will be five days late. Here's our plan.
examples.id: Pengirimannya akan terlambat lima hari. Ini rencana kami. (langsung: cocok untuk pendengar yang ingin to the point)

examples.en: I'm very sorry, Mr Sato. Because one machine broke down, the shipment will arrive five days late.
examples.id: Saya mohon maaf sekali, Pak Sato. Karena satu mesin rusak, pengirimannya akan tiba terlambat lima hari. (bentuknya tidak langsung, isinya tetap jelas)

examples.en: Sorry to bother you, but would it be possible to meet on Thursday?
examples.id: Maaf mengganggu, tapi apakah mungkin kita bertemu hari Kamis? (kesopanan negatif: tidak memaksakan)

id.title: Langsung atau tidak langsung: pilih strategi sesuai pendengar
id.explanation: Dalam komunikasi konteks rendah, pesannya sebagian besar ada di kata-kata; dalam komunikasi konteks tinggi, banyak pesan ada di hubungan, situasi dan hal yang tidak diucapkan. Kesopanan positif menunjukkan keakraban (nama depan, pujian, we); kesopanan negatif menghindari kesan memaksa (pilihan, permintaan maaf, Could you possibly…?). Sebagai kecenderungan umum, penutur Belanda, Jerman dan Australia lebih langsung, penutur Jepang, Thailand dan Indonesia lebih tidak langsung. Pilih sesuai pendengar, hubungan, di depan umum atau empat mata, dan taruhannya: sesuaikan bentuknya, isinya tetap jelas.

keyPoints.title: Bridge meaning: decode, check, reframe
keyPoints.explanation: A polite 'iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' is not a firm yes: it may be a soft no. Don't translate it word for word, and don't turn every iya into a no either. Interpret with a hedge (So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean…), check with the speaker, often privately (Could I check what you meant by…?), and confirm in writing. Reframe a blunt message so the other side can hear it (It's about the report, not about you), make an indirect message explicit for a direct listener, and don't read silence as agreement.

examples.en: So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean he has some concerns.
examples.id: Jadi kalau Pak Budi bilang 'nanti kami pertimbangkan', mungkin maksudnya ia punya beberapa keberatan.

examples.en: Could I check what you meant by 'it's a bit difficult', Mr Sato?
examples.id: Boleh saya pastikan maksud Bapak dengan 'agak sulit', Pak Sato?

examples.en: Anna's comments are about the report, not about you.
examples.id: Komentar Anna itu tentang laporannya, bukan tentang kamu.

id.title: Jembatani makna: pahami, pastikan, bingkai ulang
id.explanation: 'Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' yang sopan bukan ya yang pasti: bisa jadi itu penolakan halus. Jangan terjemahkan kata per kata, tapi jangan juga mengubah setiap iya menjadi tidak. Tafsirkan dengan hati-hati (So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean…), pastikan ke pembicaranya, sering kali empat mata (Could I check what you meant by…?), lalu konfirmasi secara tertulis. Bingkai ulang pesan yang blak-blakan supaya pihak lain bisa menerimanya (It's about the report, not about you), buat pesan yang tidak langsung menjadi jelas untuk pendengar yang lugas, dan jangan anggap diam sebagai tanda setuju.

guidedPractice.prompt: Mr Sato, a client from Japan, will visit the factory in Cikarang and asks how to give a small gift to Pak Hasan. Complete your advice with one word: 'Give it with your ___ hand, or with both hands to show extra respect.'
guidedPractice.hint: In Indonesia, giving or receiving things with the left hand is often seen as impolite.

guidedPractice.prompt: Make this explanation a tendency instead of a stereotype. Replace 'always' with one word: 'Indonesians always avoid saying no directly.'
guidedPractice.hint: A mediator explains tendencies: many, often, usually, tend to. Always, never and all turn an explanation into a stereotype.

guidedPractice.prompt: 'Sorry to bother you, but would it be possible to move our call to Thursday?' Is this positive politeness (showing closeness) or negative politeness (not imposing)? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: An apology for disturbing and a question about what's possible give the listener room to say no: that's not imposing.

guidedPractice.prompt: Anna, a Dutch manager in Jakarta, wrote 'This total is wrong.' on Dimas's spreadsheet. You soften it for Dimas but keep the message. Complete with one word: 'I think there ___ be a mistake in this total.'
guidedPractice.hint: A modal verb softens the form; the content (there's a mistake in the total) stays the same.

guidedPractice.prompt: Kate, an Australian NGO director in Lombok, asked the team 'Any objections?' and nobody spoke. You explain. Complete with one word: 'Their silence may show respect, ___ agreement.'
guidedPractice.hint: In many Indonesian settings, silence in front of a senior person can mean respect, thinking or quiet disagreement.

independentPractice.prompt: After her holiday, a colleague tells Kate: 'Wah, Bu Kate gemukan ya!' ('You've put on weight!'). Kate is shocked. Explain the norm to her in one or two sentences, without judging either side.
expected: in many indonesian workplaces comments like that are a friendly way of showing that people noticed you it isn't meant as an insult
here people often comment on weight to show attention and closeness it's not meant to be rude
in indonesia remarks about weight are often just friendly small talk they don't mean to criticise you
independentPractice.hint: Tendency (In many Indonesian workplaces…) + reason (attention, closeness) + what it isn't (not an insult) + maybe what to do (a smile is enough).

independentPractice.prompt: Rewrite 'Send me the test results today.' for Mr Sato, a senior client from Japan, using negative politeness (not imposing). One sentence.
expected: would it be possible to send me the test results today
i'm sorry to trouble you but could you possibly send the test results today
could you possibly send me the test results today if it isn't too much trouble
i was wondering if you could send me the test results today
independentPractice.hint: Use a question that gives room to say no: Would it be possible…? / Could you possibly…? / I was wondering if… You can add an apology for the trouble.

independentPractice.prompt: In a meeting, Anna tells Sari: 'Your summary is far too long. Nobody will read it.' Sari goes quiet. Privately, reframe Anna's message for Sari: keep the content, change the packaging. One or two sentences.
expected: anna's comment is about the summary not about you her point is that it needs to be shorter so people actually read it
in many dutch workplaces feedback like this is normal anna wants a shorter summary so that people will read it
it isn't personal anna thinks the summary should be much shorter shall we cut it to one page together
independentPractice.hint: Separate the message from the tone, keep the content (much shorter), give the context (Dutch directness is normal) and offer a next step.

assessment.prompt: In a team meeting in Jakarta, Anna, the Dutch manager, proposes moving the weekly meeting to 7.30 a.m. Many of the team commute two hours from Bogor and Bekasi. Pak Budi, the senior supervisor, smiles, says 'Iya, Bu, nanti kami pertimbangkan dulu,' and quickly changes the subject. Nobody else speaks. Afterwards Anna asks you: 'Great, so they agreed?' What is the likely real meaning of Pak Budi's answer: yes, no or maybe? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: no (a soft, polite no: 'nanti kami pertimbangkan' + a quick change of subject + silence from the team, and a clear reason against: a two-hour commute makes 7.30 very hard). The idea in Indonesian (tidak, penolakan halus) = 60. 'maybe' = 30 (sees that it isn't a firm yes, but misses the cues: a change of subject, silence, a strong reason against). 'yes' = 0: the node's common error, translating a polite 'iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' as a firm yes.

assessment.prompt: Pak Budi told the Dutch manager 'Kami usahakan, Bu' ('We'll try') about a Friday deadline. You don't want to guess, so after the meeting you check with him privately and politely. Complete with one word: 'Pak Budi, could I check what you ___ by "we'll try"? Anna will plan around your answer.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: meant (Could I check what you meant by …? is the bridge phrase for checking a speaker's meaning; the past form is softer and refers to what he said). 'mean' = 100 (also natural). 'intended' = 70 (understandable, but 'what you intended by' is less natural). Any other word ('said', 'want', 'promised') = 0: 'what you said by' isn't English, and 'promised' turns the check into pressure. An answer in Indonesian = 0 (the gap needs an English word).

assessment.prompt: On her first day in Jakarta, Anna, the new Dutch manager, told the team: 'Please just tell me straight. I'd rather hear bad news early.' Now you have to tell her that a supplier will miss Friday's deadline. Which strategy suits Anna better: direct or indirect? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: direct (Anna has asked for it, many Dutch workplaces are low-context, and a missed deadline is a costly matter that needs clear content: say the problem first, then the plan). The idea in Indonesian (langsung) = 60. 'indirect' = 0 (hints or a long preamble risk the bad news reaching her too late, the opposite of what she asked for).

assessment.prompt: Mr Sato, a senior client from Japan, is touring the factory in Cikarang with his team and your director. In front of everyone, he suggests a change to the packing line that you know will cost far more than he expects. You need to raise the cost. Which strategy is the better first choice here: direct or indirect? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: indirect (a senior client, in front of his own team, and a broad Japanese tendency towards high-context communication: contradicting him openly could cause loss of face. Raise it carefully, for example 'That may be a little difficult with the current budget. Could we look at the costs together after the tour?', and make the figures clear in private). The idea in Indonesian (tidak langsung) = 60. 'direct' = 0 for this context (a blunt correction in public is the risky choice; the content still has to be clear, but later and privately).

assessment.prompt: Kate, the new Australian director of an NGO in Lombok, asks why her staff still call her 'Bu Kate' after she said 'Just call me Kate'. Complete your explanation with one word: 'Here, Pak and Bu are a sign of ___, not distance. Using only your first name would feel uncomfortable for many of them, especially the younger staff.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: respect (Pak / Bu + first name is the respectful form in many Indonesian workplaces, especially towards someone older or more senior; it isn't coldness or distance). 'politeness', 'courtesy', 'deference' = 100. 'hierarchy' or 'status' = 70 (true, but misses the warm, respectful side). The idea in Indonesian (hormat) = 60. 'fear' or 'distance' = 0 (the explanation says it isn't distance; fear turns a norm into a stereotype).

assessment.prompt: On her first day in Jakarta, a new colleague asked Anna, the Dutch manager, how old she is. Anna found it a strange question. Complete your explanation with one word: 'Here, people often ask your age so they know how to ___ you: Mbak, Kak, Bu or Dik. It's friendly attention, not nosiness.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: address (in Indonesian, the word people use for you depends partly on your age compared with theirs, so the question helps them be polite). 'call' = 100. 'greet' = 70 (close, but the point is the form of address, not the greeting). 'treat' = 50 (too general). The idea in Indonesian (memanggil, menyapa) = 60. Words that make it negative (judge, control) = 0.

assessment.prompt: During Ramadan, Anna wants to hold a two-hour team lunch meeting in Jakarta. Most of the team are fasting. Complete your advice with one word: 'Many of the team will be fasting from dawn until ___, so a lunch meeting won't work. A late-afternoon meeting that ends with buka puasa together would be a nice gesture.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: sunset (during Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn until sunset; buka puasa, breaking the fast, happens at maghrib, around sunset). 'sundown', 'dusk', 'maghrib' = 100. 'evening' or 'night' = 70 (roughly right, but not precise). 'lunch', 'noon' or 'midday' = 0 (the fast lasts all day, which is exactly why a lunch meeting won't work).

material.title: Explaining a norm: tendency, reason, what to do

id.title: Menjelaskan norma: kecenderungan, alasan, apa yang dilakukan

blocks.text:
Quick recap: at C1 you explained a **cultural concept** (*sungkan, gotong royong, musyawarah, jam karet*) in four parts: an approximate translation, an example, what it isn't, and why it matters. At B2 you learnt which small-talk topics are safe, and at C1 that English uses *Mr / Ms + surname*.

Now you explain **norms**. A **norm** (norma) is an unwritten rule about how people behave: who speaks first in a meeting, how you address your boss, when a meeting really starts. People rarely notice their own norms until someone breaks them. As a mediator you explain them **in both directions**: Indonesian norms to foreign colleagues, and foreign norms to Indonesian colleagues. Four moves:
1. **The tendency**, in careful words: *In many Indonesian offices, … / People often … / In some workplaces, … / It's common to …*
2. **The reason**, the value behind it: respect, harmony, closeness, efficiency, honesty.
3. **What it doesn't mean:** *It isn't rudeness. / It doesn't mean they're not interested.*
4. **What to do:** *So it's a good idea to … / You don't have to …, but …*

id.text:
Ulang singkat: di C1 kamu sudah menjelaskan **konsep budaya** (*sungkan, gotong royong, musyawarah, jam karet*) dalam empat bagian: terjemahan kira-kira, contoh, apa yang bukan, dan kenapa itu penting. Di B2 kamu belajar topik basa-basi yang aman, dan di C1 bahwa bahasa Inggris memakai *Mr / Ms + nama belakang*.

Sekarang kamu menjelaskan **norma**. **Norma** adalah aturan tak tertulis tentang cara orang bersikap: siapa yang bicara duluan di rapat, bagaimana memanggil atasan, kapan rapat benar-benar dimulai. Orang jarang menyadari norma mereka sendiri sampai ada yang melanggarnya. Sebagai penengah, kamu menjelaskannya **ke dua arah**: norma Indonesia untuk rekan asing, dan norma asing untuk rekan Indonesia. Empat langkah:
1. **Kecenderungannya**, dengan kata-kata yang hati-hati: *In many Indonesian offices, … / People often … / In some workplaces, … / It's common to …*
2. **Alasannya**, nilai di baliknya: hormat, kerukunan, keakraban, efisiensi, kejujuran.
3. **Apa yang bukan maksudnya:** *It isn't rudeness. / It doesn't mean they're not interested.*
4. **Apa yang sebaiknya dilakukan:** *So it's a good idea to … / You don't have to …, but …*

rows.en: In many Indonesian offices, people use Pak or Bu with your first name. It's a sign of respect, so you don't need to stop them.
rows.id: Di banyak kantor di Indonesia, orang memakai Pak atau Bu dengan nama depanmu. Itu tanda hormat, jadi kamu tidak perlu melarangnya.

rows.en: In many Dutch workplaces, people disagree openly with the manager. It shows they're engaged; it isn't disrespect.
rows.id: Di banyak tempat kerja di Belanda, orang membantah manajer secara terbuka. Itu tanda mereka peduli, bukan tidak hormat.

rows.en: In Australia it's common to call even the CEO by her first name. So 'Kate' is fine, if it feels comfortable.
rows.id: Di Australia, memanggil CEO dengan nama depannya saja itu biasa. Jadi 'Kate' tidak apa-apa, kalau kamu merasa nyaman.

rows.en: Many people here will ask if you're married. It's friendly interest; a smile and 'Not yet' is enough.
rows.id: Banyak orang di sini akan bertanya apakah kamu sudah menikah. Itu bentuk perhatian; senyum dan 'Belum' sudah cukup.

blocks.text:
**Tendency, not stereotype.** *Indonesians are always late* or *The Dutch are rude* are labels; *At some informal events, start times are flexible* and *Many Dutch colleagues give feedback very directly* are explanations.
- Swap **always / never / all / they** for **many / often / tend to / in some workplaces**.
- Never rank cultures: no *better, more professional, more advanced, backward*. **Direct isn't rude, and indirect isn't dishonest:** both are ways of being polite.
- People differ inside a country too: a Jakarta startup, a ministry in Mataram and a family firm in Surabaya have different norms. Explain the norm, then let the person surprise you.

id.text:
**Kecenderungan, bukan stereotip.** *Indonesians are always late* atau *The Dutch are rude* adalah label; *At some informal events, start times are flexible* dan *Many Dutch colleagues give feedback very directly* adalah penjelasan.
- Ganti **always / never / all / they** dengan **many / often / tend to / in some workplaces**.
- Jangan pernah membuat peringkat budaya: tidak ada *better, more professional, more advanced, backward*. **Lugas itu bukan kasar, dan tidak langsung itu bukan tidak jujur:** keduanya cara bersikap sopan.
- Orang dalam satu negara pun berbeda: startup di Jakarta, kementerian di Mataram dan perusahaan keluarga di Surabaya punya norma yang berbeda. Jelaskan normanya, lalu biarkan orangnya mengejutkanmu.

blocks.prompt: In a meeting in Jakarta, Anna, the Dutch manager, openly disagreed with the regional director. Afterwards, Rina asks you: 'Isn't that very rude?' Which explanation is best?
options: Yes. Dutch people don't respect their bosses.
In many Dutch workplaces, disagreeing openly with a senior person is normal and even expected: it shows you care about the work. It wasn't a personal attack, and the director didn't take it as one.
Anna probably wants the director's job, so she's trying to make him look bad.
blocks.explain: The second answer gives the tendency (*In many Dutch workplaces*), the reason (it shows you care about the work) and what it doesn't mean (not a personal attack). The first is a stereotype that judges a whole culture; the third invents a motive instead of explaining a norm.

id.prompt: Dalam rapat di Jakarta, Anna, manajer asal Belanda, secara terbuka membantah direktur regional. Sesudahnya Rina bertanya padamu: 'Bukankah itu kasar sekali?' Penjelasan mana yang terbaik?
id.explain: Jawaban kedua menyebut kecenderungannya (*In many Dutch workplaces*), alasannya (menunjukkan kamu peduli pada pekerjaan) dan apa yang bukan maksudnya (bukan serangan pribadi). Yang pertama stereotip yang menghakimi satu budaya; yang ketiga mengarang motif alih-alih menjelaskan norma.

id.title: Norma yang sering menimbulkan salah paham

blocks.text:
These are **broad tendencies**, useful as a map, not as rules about people:
- **Address and hierarchy.** In Indonesia, **Pak / Bu + first name** (*Pak Budi, Bu Ani*): many Indonesians have no family name, and some have only one name, so *Mr Budi* is correct English for an Indonesian colleague. For most Westerners, it's **Mr / Ms + surname** (*Ms de Vries*), never *Mr John*. In Australia and the Netherlands, **first names** are common even with the CEO; in many traditional German companies, people still use *Herr / Frau* + surname.
- **Age.** Indonesians often ask your age partly to know how to address you (*Mbak, Kak, Dik, Bu, Pak*).
- **Time.** Work meetings, flights and interviews in Indonesia start on time; *jam karet* is about some informal events. In many Dutch, German and Japanese workplaces a deadline is a promise: if it might slip, people expect to hear early, not on the day.
- **Face and criticism.** **Face** (muka, harga diri) is how others see you. In many Indonesian, Japanese and Thai settings, criticism is given in private; in many Dutch workplaces, frank feedback in a meeting is normal.
- **Saying no.** *Nanti kami pertimbangkan, kami usahakan, agak sulit, Pak* and a Japanese client's *That may be a little difficult* can all be soft no's.
- **Small talk.** Age, salary, marriage and weight are friendly topics for many Indonesians, but sensitive in many Western workplaces.
- **Religion at work.** Many Muslim colleagues pray at set times (a prayer takes about 10–15 minutes, often in the *musholla*, the office prayer room). On **Fridays**, many Muslim men go to the mosque around midday, so many workplaces take a longer break (roughly 11.30 to 1). In **Ramadan**, many colleagues fast from dawn to sunset, offices often close earlier, and teams share *buka puasa* (breaking the fast). When you host, check the food is **halal**.
- **Gifts and hospitality.** Colleagues bring *oleh-oleh* from a trip; Japanese visitors often bring *omiyage*, a similar gift. In Indonesia and Japan, gifts are often opened later, not in front of the giver; many Australians open them straight away.
- **Hands.** Give, receive and eat with the **right hand** (both hands = extra respect). Japanese business cards are given and received with **both hands**.

id.text:
Ini **kecenderungan umum**, berguna sebagai peta, bukan aturan tentang orang:
- **Panggilan dan hierarki.** Di Indonesia, **Pak / Bu + nama depan** (*Pak Budi, Bu Ani*): banyak orang Indonesia tidak punya nama keluarga, bahkan ada yang namanya hanya satu kata, jadi *Mr Budi* itu bahasa Inggris yang benar untuk rekan Indonesia. Untuk kebanyakan orang Barat, pakai **Mr / Ms + nama belakang** (*Ms de Vries*), jangan *Mr John*. Di Australia dan Belanda, **nama depan** biasa dipakai bahkan kepada CEO; di banyak perusahaan Jerman yang tradisional, orang masih memakai *Herr / Frau* + nama belakang.
- **Usia.** Orang Indonesia sering menanyakan usia antara lain supaya tahu cara memanggilmu (*Mbak, Kak, Dik, Bu, Pak*).
- **Waktu.** Rapat kerja, penerbangan dan wawancara di Indonesia dimulai tepat waktu; *jam karet* itu soal sebagian acara santai. Di banyak tempat kerja di Belanda, Jerman dan Jepang, tenggat adalah janji: kalau mungkin meleset, orang ingin tahu dari awal, bukan pada harinya.
- **Muka dan kritik.** **Face** (muka, harga diri) adalah cara orang lain memandangmu. Di banyak lingkungan Indonesia, Jepang dan Thailand, kritik disampaikan empat mata; di banyak tempat kerja di Belanda, masukan yang blak-blakan di rapat itu biasa.
- **Menolak.** *Nanti kami pertimbangkan, kami usahakan, agak sulit, Pak* dan ucapan klien Jepang *That may be a little difficult* semuanya bisa berarti penolakan halus.
- **Basa-basi.** Usia, gaji, pernikahan dan berat badan adalah topik ramah bagi banyak orang Indonesia, tapi sensitif di banyak tempat kerja Barat.
- **Agama di tempat kerja.** Banyak rekan Muslim salat pada waktu tertentu (sekali salat sekitar 10–15 menit, sering di *musholla* kantor). Pada **hari Jumat**, banyak laki-laki Muslim ke masjid sekitar tengah hari, jadi banyak kantor memberi istirahat lebih panjang (kira-kira 11.30 sampai 13.00). Saat **Ramadan**, banyak rekan berpuasa dari subuh sampai matahari terbenam, kantor sering tutup lebih awal, dan tim berbuka puasa bersama. Saat menjamu, pastikan makanannya **halal**.
- **Hadiah dan keramahan.** Rekan membawa *oleh-oleh* dari perjalanan; tamu dari Jepang sering membawa *omiyage*, hadiah yang mirip. Di Indonesia dan Jepang, hadiah sering dibuka belakangan, tidak di depan pemberinya; banyak orang Australia langsung membukanya.
- **Tangan.** Memberi, menerima dan makan dengan **tangan kanan** (dua tangan = lebih hormat). Kartu nama Jepang diberikan dan diterima dengan **dua tangan**.

rows.en: You can call him Pak Budi. Budi is his first name, and many Indonesians don't have a family name.
rows.id: Kamu bisa memanggilnya Pak Budi. Budi itu nama depannya, dan banyak orang Indonesia tidak punya nama keluarga.

rows.en: If the deadline might slip, tell Anna on Monday, not on Friday afternoon.
rows.id: Kalau tenggatnya mungkin meleset, beri tahu Anna hari Senin, bukan Jumat sore.

rows.en: It's best to give Pak Hendra that feedback one to one, not in front of his team.
rows.id: Sebaiknya masukan itu disampaikan ke Pak Hendra empat mata, bukan di depan timnya.

rows.en: Mr Sato may not open your gift in front of you. It's polite, not a sign he doesn't like it.
rows.id: Pak Sato mungkin tidak membuka hadiahmu di depanmu. Itu sopan, bukan tanda ia tidak suka.

blocks.text: **Two scales, not one.** Being **direct** and being **informal** are different things. Many German colleagues are direct but formal (*Herr Dr. Weber*); many Australians are direct and informal (*G'day, Kate here*); many Japanese clients are indirect and formal; many Indonesian colleagues are indirect, use *Pak / Bu*, and still ask warm personal questions. So don't explain a whole culture with one word like *formal* or *relaxed*.

id.text: **Dua skala, bukan satu.** **Lugas** dan **santai** itu hal yang berbeda. Banyak rekan Jerman lugas tapi formal (*Herr Dr. Weber*); banyak orang Australia lugas dan santai (*G'day, Kate here*); banyak klien Jepang tidak langsung dan formal; banyak rekan Indonesia tidak langsung, memakai *Pak / Bu*, tapi tetap menanyakan hal pribadi dengan hangat. Jadi jangan jelaskan satu budaya dengan satu kata seperti *formal* atau *santai*.

blocks.prompt: At the end of his visit to the factory in Cikarang, Pak Hasan gives Mr Sato a batik shirt. Mr Sato thanks him warmly but doesn't open it. Kate, an Australian guest, whispers: 'Oh no, he doesn't like it.' What do you tell her?
options: In Japan, and often in Indonesia too, gifts are usually opened later, not in front of the giver. It's polite, not a sign that he doesn't like it.
You're right. Japanese people never like batik.
He can't open it: in Japan, gifts from clients belong to the company.
blocks.explain: The first answer explains the norm (gifts are often opened later) and what it doesn't mean (not dislike). The second is a stereotype with *never*; the third invents a rule. Note the contrast: many Australians open a gift straight away to show they're pleased, so Kate's reading is natural for her, just not for this situation.

id.prompt: Di akhir kunjungannya ke pabrik di Cikarang, Pak Hasan memberi Pak Sato kemeja batik. Pak Sato berterima kasih dengan hangat tapi tidak membukanya. Kate, tamu dari Australia, berbisik: 'Oh no, he doesn't like it.' Apa yang kamu katakan padanya?
id.explain: Jawaban pertama menjelaskan normanya (hadiah sering dibuka belakangan) dan apa yang bukan maksudnya (bukan tidak suka). Yang kedua stereotip dengan *never*; yang ketiga mengarang aturan. Perhatikan bedanya: banyak orang Australia langsung membuka hadiah untuk menunjukkan rasa senang, jadi tafsiran Kate wajar baginya, hanya tidak cocok untuk situasi ini.

material.title: Direct and indirect: two ways to be polite

id.title: Langsung dan tidak langsung: dua cara bersikap sopan

blocks.text:
Two simple ideas explain a lot of cross-cultural confusion.

**1. Low-context and high-context.** The anthropologist Edward T. Hall noticed that in some cultures the message is mostly **in the words** (**low-context**, konteks rendah: say what you mean, and if it isn't said, it isn't meant). In others, much of the message is **in the situation**: the relationship, who is present, what is *not* said (**high-context**, konteks tinggi: the listener is expected to read between the lines). As broad tendencies, Dutch, German and Australian speakers lean low-context and direct; Japanese, Thai and Indonesian speakers lean high-context and indirect. Americans are usually explicit, but often wrap criticism in praise.

**2. Positive and negative politeness.** The researchers Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson described two ways of being polite:
- **Positive politeness** = showing **closeness**: first names, compliments, jokes, *we*, interest in the person (*How's your family?*). Much Indonesian *basa-basi* and Australian friendliness work this way.
- **Negative politeness** = **not imposing**: giving options, apologising for the trouble, softening requests (*Sorry to bother you, but could you possibly …?*). British English and Japanese business language use a lot of it.

**Negative** here doesn't mean bad: it means keeping a respectful distance. Most people use both, depending on the listener.

id.text:
Dua gagasan sederhana menjelaskan banyak kebingungan lintas budaya.

**1. Konteks rendah dan konteks tinggi.** Antropolog Edward T. Hall memperhatikan bahwa di sebagian budaya pesannya sebagian besar ada **di kata-kata** (**low-context**, konteks rendah: katakan maksudmu, dan kalau tidak diucapkan, berarti tidak dimaksudkan). Di budaya lain, banyak pesan ada **di situasinya**: hubungan, siapa yang hadir, apa yang *tidak* diucapkan (**high-context**, konteks tinggi: pendengar diharapkan menangkap yang tersirat). Sebagai kecenderungan umum, penutur Belanda, Jerman dan Australia condong ke konteks rendah dan lugas; penutur Jepang, Thailand dan Indonesia condong ke konteks tinggi dan tidak langsung. Orang Amerika biasanya eksplisit, tapi sering membungkus kritik dengan pujian.

**2. Kesopanan positif dan negatif.** Peneliti Penelope Brown dan Stephen Levinson menggambarkan dua cara bersikap sopan:
- **Kesopanan positif** = menunjukkan **keakraban**: nama depan, pujian, bercanda, *we*, perhatian pada orangnya (*How's your family?*). Banyak basa-basi Indonesia dan keramahan Australia bekerja seperti ini.
- **Kesopanan negatif** = **tidak memaksakan**: memberi pilihan, minta maaf karena merepotkan, melunakkan permintaan (*Sorry to bother you, but could you possibly …?*). Bahasa Inggris British dan bahasa bisnis Jepang banyak memakainya.

**Negatif** di sini bukan berarti buruk: artinya menjaga jarak dengan hormat. Kebanyakan orang memakai keduanya, tergantung pendengarnya.

rows.en: The report needs more data before Friday.
rows.id: Laporannya butuh data tambahan sebelum Jumat.

rows.en: Great work in the field this week, everyone! Let's make the report as strong as the fieldwork.
rows.id: Kerja lapangan minggu ini hebat, semuanya! Ayo buat laporannya sekuat kerja lapangannya.

rows.en: I'm sorry to trouble you, but would it be possible to add a little more data?
rows.id: Maaf merepotkan, tapi apakah mungkin datanya ditambah sedikit?

rows.en: The figures for Bandung look a little thin at the moment.
rows.id: Angka untuk Bandung kelihatannya masih agak tipis.
rows.note: high-context hint: the listener must infer 'add data'

id.note: kode halus konteks tinggi: pendengar harus menangkap 'tambah datanya'

blocks.text:
**Choosing the strategy.** Ask four questions: **Who is listening** (their tendency, and what they've told you they prefer)? **What's the relationship** (senior, client, new, close)? **Public or private?** **What are the stakes?** Then follow the rule of thumb: **adapt the form, keep the content clear**. A Japanese client can get an apology, a reason and careful words, but the delivery date must still be in the sentence. A Dutch manager can get the bad news in the first line, but a *thank you* doesn't hurt.

Both extremes fail: a long, soft preamble can leave a Dutch manager asking *So what's the point?*, while a blunt correction in front of his team can make a senior Japanese client lose face. And from C2 implied meaning: safety, money and deadlines need clear content for everyone.

id.text:
**Memilih strategi.** Ajukan empat pertanyaan: **Siapa pendengarnya** (kecenderungannya, dan apa yang ia bilang ia sukai)? **Bagaimana hubungannya** (atasan, klien, orang baru, akrab)? **Di depan umum atau empat mata?** **Seberapa besar taruhannya?** Lalu ikuti pegangan ini: **sesuaikan bentuknya, isinya tetap jelas**. Klien Jepang bisa mendapat permintaan maaf, alasan dan kata-kata yang hati-hati, tapi tanggal pengirimannya tetap harus ada di kalimat itu. Manajer Belanda bisa mendapat kabar buruknya di baris pertama, tapi ucapan *thank you* tidak ada ruginya.

Dua ekstrem sama-sama gagal: pembukaan yang panjang dan halus bisa membuat manajer Belanda bertanya *So what's the point?*, sedangkan koreksi blak-blakan di depan timnya bisa membuat klien senior Jepang kehilangan muka. Dan dari pelajaran C2 tentang makna tersirat: keselamatan, uang dan tenggat butuh isi yang jelas untuk siapa pun.

blocks.prompt: Kate, the Australian director of an NGO in Lombok, asks you to tell the local field team that their reports have too many mistakes. The team are proud of their fieldwork and several are much younger than the coordinator. Which approach fits the team best?
options: Read the list of mistakes aloud at the Monday team meeting so everyone learns.
Thank the team for the fieldwork, then go through the corrections with each writer privately, with clear examples of what to change.
Say nothing: they'll notice the mistakes themselves eventually.
blocks.explain: The second approach adapts the form (thanks first, privately, which protects face) and keeps the content clear (concrete corrections). Reading mistakes aloud in public risks loss of face; saying nothing loses the message completely.

id.prompt: Kate, direktur LSM dari Australia di Lombok, memintamu memberi tahu tim lapangan setempat bahwa laporan mereka terlalu banyak kesalahan. Tim itu bangga dengan kerja lapangannya, dan beberapa jauh lebih muda dari koordinatornya. Cara mana yang paling cocok untuk tim ini?
id.explain: Cara kedua menyesuaikan bentuknya (terima kasih dulu, empat mata, sehingga menjaga muka) dan isinya tetap jelas (koreksi yang konkret). Membacakan kesalahan di depan umum berisiko membuat orang kehilangan muka; diam saja membuat pesannya hilang sama sekali.
options: Bacakan daftar kesalahan pada rapat Senin agar semua belajar.
Apresiasi kerja lapangannya, lalu bahas koreksi secara pribadi dengan tiap penulis dan beri contoh perubahan yang jelas.
Tidak perlu mengatakan apa-apa: nanti mereka sadar sendiri.

blocks.text:
The most expensive misunderstanding in this lesson: a foreign manager proposes something, an Indonesian colleague smiles and says **Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan** (*Yes, we'll consider it*), and the manager writes *Agreed!* in the minutes. In many Indonesian settings that answer may be a **soft no**: *iya* often means *I hear you*, and *we'll consider it* avoids refusing a senior person openly (out of *sungkan*). The same family: *kami usahakan* (we'll try), *agak sulit, Pak* (it's a bit difficult) and a Japanese client's *That may be a little difficult*.

The opposite happens too: a Dutch or Australian colleague's *No, that won't work* is often the **start** of a discussion, not hostility.

As a mediator, don't translate word for word, and don't guess for the speaker either. Three moves:
1. **Interpret, with a hedge:** *So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean he has some concerns.*
2. **Check with the speaker**, often privately: *Could I check what you meant by …? / Just so I'm sure I've understood: … ? / What would make this work for your team?*
3. **Confirm in writing:** *Just to confirm, we'll start the new schedule on 1 May. Is that right?*

id.text:
Salah paham yang paling mahal di pelajaran ini: manajer asing mengusulkan sesuatu, rekan Indonesia tersenyum dan berkata **Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan**, lalu sang manajer menulis *Agreed!* di notulen. Di banyak lingkungan Indonesia, jawaban itu bisa jadi **penolakan halus**: *iya* sering berarti *aku dengar*, dan *nanti kami pertimbangkan* menghindari menolak atasan secara terang-terangan (karena *sungkan*). Satu keluarga dengannya: *kami usahakan*, *agak sulit, Pak*, dan ucapan klien Jepang *That may be a little difficult*.

Kebalikannya juga terjadi: *No, that won't work* dari rekan Belanda atau Australia sering merupakan **awal** diskusi, bukan permusuhan.

Sebagai penengah, jangan terjemahkan kata per kata, dan jangan juga menebak-nebak untuk pembicaranya. Tiga langkah:
1. **Tafsirkan, dengan hati-hati:** *So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean he has some concerns.*
2. **Pastikan ke pembicaranya**, sering kali empat mata: *Could I check what you meant by …? / Just so I'm sure I've understood: … ? / What would make this work for your team?*
3. **Konfirmasi secara tertulis:** *Just to confirm, we'll start the new schedule on 1 May. Is that right?*

rows.en: So when Pak Budi says 'we'll consider it', it may mean the team has some concerns.
rows.id: Jadi kalau Pak Budi bilang 'nanti kami pertimbangkan', mungkin maksudnya timnya punya beberapa keberatan.

rows.en: Could I check what you meant by 'it's a bit difficult', Mr Sato?
rows.id: Boleh saya pastikan maksud Bapak dengan 'agak sulit', Pak Sato?

rows.en: What would make the new schedule work for your team?
rows.id: Apa yang bisa membuat jadwal baru ini cocok untuk timmu?
rows.note: an open question: room to raise concerns without saying no

id.note: pertanyaan terbuka: memberi ruang menyampaikan keberatan tanpa bilang tidak

rows.en: When Anna says 'No, that won't work', she's usually inviting you to argue your case.
rows.id: Kalau Anna bilang 'No, that won't work', biasanya ia justru mengajakmu mempertahankan pendapatmu.

blocks.text:
**The common error:** translating *Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan* as *Yes, we agree*. Say **may**, then **check**.
- **Don't overcorrect:** not every *iya* is a no. Sometimes they really will consider it.
- **Don't expose the speaker:** saying *He means no* in front of Pak Budi makes him lose face. Check with him privately.
- **Insyaallah** (*if God wills*) is a sincere expression of faith. Depending on the context it can mean *yes*, *I'll try* or a polite *maybe*: treat it with respect, and check the plan, not the faith.
- A **closed** question (*So you agree?*) forces a public yes. An **open** one (*What would make this work?*) lets people raise concerns.

id.text:
**Kesalahan yang umum:** menerjemahkan *Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan* menjadi *Yes, we agree*. Pakai **may**, lalu **pastikan**.
- **Jangan berlebihan:** tidak setiap *iya* berarti tidak. Kadang mereka memang akan mempertimbangkannya.
- **Jangan mempermalukan pembicaranya:** bilang *He means no* di depan Pak Budi membuatnya kehilangan muka. Pastikan dengannya empat mata.
- **Insyaallah** adalah ungkapan iman yang tulus. Tergantung konteksnya, artinya bisa *ya*, *saya usahakan* atau *mungkin* yang sopan: hormati itu, dan yang kamu pastikan adalah rencananya, bukan imannya.
- Pertanyaan **tertutup** (*So you agree?*) memaksa orang bilang ya di depan umum. Pertanyaan **terbuka** (*What would make this work?*) memberi ruang untuk menyampaikan keberatan.

blocks.prompt: Anna asks Bu Ani whether the Surabaya branch can switch to the new software by the end of the month. Bu Ani answers: 'Kami usahakan, Bu.' Anna is happy. Later you talk to Bu Ani privately. Which question is the best bridge?
options: So you promise it'll be done by the 30th?
Why can't you just say yes or no?
Is there anything that might make the end of the month hard? If there is, we can tell Anna now and plan for it.
blocks.explain: The third question is open and private, gives Bu Ani room to name a problem without refusing anyone, and links it to a plan. The first is a closed question that forces a yes; the second criticises her way of speaking instead of finding out what she means.

id.prompt: Anna bertanya kepada Bu Ani apakah cabang Surabaya bisa beralih ke software baru paling lambat akhir bulan. Bu Ani menjawab: 'Kami usahakan, Bu.' Anna senang. Belakangan kamu berbicara dengan Bu Ani empat mata. Pertanyaan mana yang paling tepat sebagai jembatan?
id.explain: Pertanyaan ketiga terbuka dan empat mata, memberi Bu Ani ruang menyebut masalah tanpa menolak siapa pun, dan mengaitkannya dengan rencana. Yang pertama pertanyaan tertutup yang memaksa jawaban ya; yang kedua mengkritik cara bicaranya alih-alih mencari tahu maksudnya.

material.title: Reframing blunt messages and reading silence

id.title: Membingkai ulang pesan blak-blakan dan membaca diam

blocks.text:
**Reframing** (membingkai ulang) means keeping the **content** of a message and changing its **packaging** so the other side can hear it. It works in both directions:
- **Blunt → high-context listener.** Separate the message from the tone, give the context, turn it into a next step: *Anna's comments are about the report, not about you. In many Dutch workplaces, feedback like this is normal. Her main point is that the analysis needs more data. Shall we look at which figures to add?*
- **Indirect → direct listener.** Make the hidden message explicit, kindly: *What Mr Sato is telling us, politely, is that the price is too high for his company this year.*

Two things a mediator never does: **change the content** (*Don't worry, she liked it* when she didn't) and **take sides** (*Anna is too harsh*).

**Silence** also needs bridging. In many Indonesian, Japanese and Thai settings, silence in a meeting may mean people are **thinking**, showing **respect** to a senior person, or **disagreeing quietly**. In many Australian, Dutch or American meetings, silence after *Any objections?* is read as **agreement**. Bridge it: ask people **by name**, give **time** to think, use small groups or written input, and follow up **privately**. With a Japanese client, a pause before an answer is often thinking time: wait, don't fill it.

id.text:
**Membingkai ulang** (reframing) berarti mempertahankan **isi** pesan dan mengubah **kemasannya** supaya pihak lain bisa menerimanya. Ini berlaku ke dua arah:
- **Blak-blakan → pendengar konteks tinggi.** Pisahkan pesan dari nadanya, beri konteks, ubah menjadi langkah berikutnya: *Anna's comments are about the report, not about you. In many Dutch workplaces, feedback like this is normal. Her main point is that the analysis needs more data. Shall we look at which figures to add?*
- **Tidak langsung → pendengar lugas.** Jadikan pesan tersembunyi itu jelas, dengan ramah: *What Mr Sato is telling us, politely, is that the price is too high for his company this year.*

Dua hal yang tidak pernah dilakukan penengah: **mengubah isinya** (*Don't worry, she liked it* padahal tidak) dan **memihak** (*Anna is too harsh*).

**Diam** juga perlu dijembatani. Di banyak lingkungan Indonesia, Jepang dan Thailand, diam dalam rapat bisa berarti orang sedang **berpikir**, menunjukkan **hormat** kepada atasan, atau **tidak setuju diam-diam**. Di banyak rapat di Australia, Belanda atau Amerika, diam setelah *Any objections?* dianggap **setuju**. Jembatani: tanyai orang **dengan menyebut namanya**, beri **waktu** berpikir, pakai kelompok kecil atau masukan tertulis, dan tindak lanjuti **empat mata**. Dengan klien Jepang, jeda sebelum menjawab sering berarti waktu berpikir: tunggu, jangan diisi.

rows.en: What Pak Hendra is telling us, politely, is that the field staff need Saturdays with their families.
rows.id: Yang disampaikan Pak Hendra, dengan sopan, adalah bahwa staf lapangan butuh hari Sabtu bersama keluarga mereka.

rows.en: It isn't personal. Her main point is that the summary should fit on one page.
rows.id: Ini bukan soal pribadi. Poin utamanya adalah ringkasannya harus muat satu halaman.

rows.en: In this team, silence may mean people are still thinking, not that they agree.
rows.id: Di tim ini, diam bisa berarti orang masih berpikir, bukan berarti setuju.

rows.en: Rina, you know the field sites best. What do you think?
rows.id: Rina, kamu yang paling tahu lokasi lapangannya. Bagaimana menurutmu?

blocks.text:
**Reframing checklist:** same facts? same request? nobody blamed? a next step? If the answer to all four is yes, you've changed only the packaging.

**Indonesian trap:** wanting to protect a colleague's feelings, it's tempting to drop the bad part (*Anna bilang bagus kok*). That isn't mediation: the problem comes back later, bigger. Soften the form, never the facts.

id.text:
**Daftar cek membingkai ulang:** faktanya sama? permintaannya sama? tidak ada yang disalahkan? ada langkah berikutnya? Kalau keempatnya ya, yang kamu ubah hanya kemasannya.

**Jebakan orang Indonesia:** karena ingin menjaga perasaan rekan, kita tergoda membuang bagian yang tidak enak (*Anna bilang bagus kok*). Itu bukan mediasi: masalahnya akan kembali nanti, lebih besar. Lunakkan bentuknya, jangan faktanya.

blocks.prompt: At a planning meeting in Lombok, Kate asks: 'Any objections to moving the village visits to Saturdays? No? Great, that's settled.' Nobody spoke, and Pak Hendra, the senior coordinator, was in the room. After the meeting, what's the best thing to tell Kate?
options: In this team, silence in front of you and Pak Hendra may not mean agreement. Could we ask a few people individually before we finalise it?
Everyone agreed, because nobody said anything.
The team never tells the truth in meetings, so don't bother asking them.
blocks.explain: The first answer interprets the silence with a hedge (*may not mean agreement*), gives the reason (two senior people were present) and proposes a check. The second reads silence as agreement, the Australian default; the third is a stereotype that blames the team.

id.prompt: Dalam rapat perencanaan di Lombok, Kate bertanya: 'Any objections to moving the village visits to Saturdays? No? Great, that's settled.' Tidak ada yang bicara, dan Pak Hendra, koordinator senior, ada di ruangan itu. Setelah rapat, apa hal terbaik untuk disampaikan kepada Kate?
id.explain: Jawaban pertama menafsirkan diam itu dengan hati-hati (*may not mean agreement*), menyebut alasannya (ada dua orang senior di ruangan) dan mengusulkan untuk memastikan. Yang kedua menganggap diam berarti setuju, kebiasaan umum di Australia; yang ketiga stereotip yang menyalahkan tim.

flashcards.front: Norma (aturan tak tertulis) — jelaskan dengan 4 langkah
flashcards.back: tendency + reason + what it isn't + what to do
many, often, tend to, in some workplaces (not always / never / all)
low-context: the message is in the words; high-context: much of it is in the situation
positive: showing closeness; negative: not imposing
Adapt the form, keep the content clear.

flashcards.front: 'Iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' → untuk manajer asing
flashcards.back: It may mean they have some concerns. Let me check with Pak Budi.
Could I check what you meant by …?

resources.title: Business Speaker Erin Meyer: The Language of Negative Feedback
resources.note: A 7-minute talk by Erin Meyer, author of The Culture Map, on how differently cultures give negative feedback, from very direct (for example many Dutch managers) to much softer styles, and how to read feedback from another culture. Native-speed English; remember that her country examples are broad tendencies.

id.note: Ceramah 7 menit oleh Erin Meyer, penulis The Culture Map, tentang betapa berbedanya cara tiap budaya menyampaikan masukan negatif, dari yang sangat lugas (misalnya banyak manajer Belanda) sampai yang jauh lebih halus, dan cara membaca masukan dari budaya lain. Bahasa Inggris kecepatan penutur asli; ingat bahwa contoh negaranya adalah kecenderungan umum.

resources.title: Don't assume silence is awkward if you want inclusive international meetings
resources.note: A 2-minute clip in which Erin Meyer explains why silence in meetings feels awkward in some cultures and valuable in others, and how to include everyone. Short and clear.

id.note: Klip 2 menit; Erin Meyer menjelaskan kenapa diam dalam rapat terasa canggung di sebagian budaya tapi berharga di budaya lain, dan cara melibatkan semua orang. Singkat dan jelas.

id.intro: Di C1 kamu sudah menjelaskan konsep Indonesia seperti sungkan dan musyawarah, dan membantu dua rekan yang berbeda pendapat. Sekarang kamu menjadi jembatan antarbudaya: menjelaskan bagaimana orang cenderung bersikap dan kenapa, memilih kesopanan langsung atau tidak langsung untuk tiap pendengar, dan memastikan 'iya, nanti kami pertimbangkan' yang sopan tidak didengar sebagai ya yang pasti.
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana menjelaskan jam karet atau sungkan kepada manajer asing tanpa membuat orang Indonesia terdengar buruk?
Apa beda kesopanan positif dan negatif, dengan contoh di tempat kerja?
Bagaimana memberi tahu manajer Belanda-ku bahwa 'nanti kami pertimbangkan' kemungkinan berarti tidak, tanpa mempermalukan rekanku?
Apakah boleh memanggil bos orang Australia dengan nama depannya saja?

assessment.ccm-1: Dalam rapat tim di Jakarta, Anna, manajer asal Belanda, mengusulkan rapat mingguan dipindah ke pukul 7.30 pagi. Banyak anggota tim pulang-pergi dua jam dari Bogor dan Bekasi. Pak Budi, supervisor senior, tersenyum, berkata 'Iya, Bu, nanti kami pertimbangkan dulu,' lalu cepat-cepat mengganti topik. Tidak ada orang lain yang bicara. Setelah itu Anna bertanya padamu: 'Great, so they agreed?' Apa kemungkinan makna sebenarnya dari jawaban Pak Budi: yes, no atau maybe? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ccm-2: Pak Budi berkata kepada manajer asal Belanda 'Kami usahakan, Bu' ('We'll try') tentang tenggat hari Jumat. Kamu tidak mau menebak-nebak, jadi setelah rapat kamu memastikan kepadanya empat mata dengan sopan. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: 'Pak Budi, could I check what you ___ by "we'll try"? Anna will plan around your answer.'
assessment.ccm-3: Pada hari pertamanya di Jakarta, Anna, manajer baru asal Belanda, berkata kepada tim: 'Please just tell me straight. I'd rather hear bad news early.' Sekarang kamu harus memberitahunya bahwa seorang pemasok akan melewatkan tenggat hari Jumat. Strategi mana yang lebih cocok untuk Anna: direct atau indirect? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ccm-4: Pak Sato, klien senior dari Jepang, sedang berkeliling pabrik di Cikarang bersama timnya dan direkturmu. Di depan semua orang, ia mengusulkan perubahan pada lini pengemasan yang kamu tahu akan jauh lebih mahal dari perkiraannya. Kamu perlu menyampaikan soal biayanya. Strategi mana yang lebih tepat sebagai pilihan pertama di sini: direct atau indirect? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ccm-5: Kate, direktur baru asal Australia di sebuah LSM di Lombok, bertanya kenapa stafnya tetap memanggilnya 'Bu Kate' padahal ia sudah bilang 'Just call me Kate'. Lengkapi penjelasanmu dengan satu kata: 'Here, Pak and Bu are a sign of ___, not distance. Using only your first name would feel uncomfortable for many of them, especially the younger staff.'
assessment.ccm-6: Pada hari pertamanya di Jakarta, seorang rekan baru menanyakan umur Anna, manajer asal Belanda. Anna merasa itu pertanyaan aneh. Lengkapi penjelasanmu dengan satu kata: 'Here, people often ask your age so they know how to ___ you: Mbak, Kak, Bu or Dik. It's friendly attention, not nosiness.'
assessment.ccm-7: Saat Ramadan, Anna ingin mengadakan rapat makan siang tim selama dua jam di Jakarta. Sebagian besar anggota tim berpuasa. Lengkapi saranmu dengan satu kata: 'Many of the team will be fasting from dawn until ___, so a lunch meeting won't work. A late-afternoon meeting that ends with buka puasa together would be a nice gesture.'
